# Trimming adapters and low-quality bases {#sec-trimming}

**Rule:** `trim` · **Tool:** Trim Galore 0.6.10 (a wrapper around Cutadapt) ·
**Input:** raw R1 and R2 FASTQ · **Output:** `{sample}_R1_trimmed.fastq.gz`,
`{sample}_R2_trimmed.fastq.gz`, and a trimming report per read

## The problem it solves

Two kinds of bases in a read are not useful:

1. **Adapter.** When the insert is shorter than the read length, the read
   continues into the adapter ([After submission](after-submission.qmd#sequencing-reading-the-fragment-from-both-ends)).
   Those bases are not in the genome and make reads fail to align or align badly.
2. **Low-quality bases**, usually at the 3' end of the read, where the
   sequencer is least confident.

Trimming cuts these off the end of each read, and throws away reads that
become too short to place reliably.

```
before:  GATTTGGGGTTCAAAGCAGTATCGATCAAATAG AGATCGGAAGAGC ACACGTCTGAACTCCAGTCAC
                  your insert                 └──── Illumina adapter ────┘
after:   GATTTGGGGTTCAAAGCAGTATCGATCAAATAG
```

## What bagPipes runs

```bash
module load trim_galore/0.6.10
trim_galore -o output/trim --paired  sample_R1_001.fastq.gz  sample_R2_001.fastq.gz
# renames *_val_1.fq.gz -> {sampleName}_R1_trimmed.fastq.gz (and _val_2 -> _R2)
```

Only one option is set: `--paired`. Everything else uses Trim Galore's
defaults:

| Default | What it does |
|---|---|
| Adapter **auto-detection** | Looks at the first 1 million reads for the Illumina, Nextera and small-RNA adapter starts, and uses whichever is most common (usually Illumina, `AGATCGGAAGAGC`) |
| `-q 20` | Trims bases with quality below 20 from the 3' end |
| `--stringency 1` | Even a single base matching the adapter at the very end is trimmed |
| `-e 0.1` | Allows 10 % mismatches when matching the adapter |
| `--length 20` | Discards reads shorter than 20 bp after trimming |
| `--paired` | Keeps R1 and R2 in step: **if either read of a pair is too short, both are removed** |

::: {.callout-note}
## Why "paired" matters

Aligners expect read 1,000 in the R1 file to be the mate of read 1,000 in the
R2 file. If you trimmed R1 and R2 separately and one lost a read, every
pair after it would be mismatched. `--paired` prevents this.
:::

## Reading the trimming report

Trim Galore writes a text report per read file. Before Snakemake deletes it (it is
`temp()`; see [the map](pipeline-map.qmd#the-output-folder)), MultiQC pulls
out the key numbers:

- **Reads with adapters**: % of reads where adapter was found. Depends on
  insert size; 10–40 % is common for `2x100`/`2x150`.
- **Bases quality-trimmed** and **total written (filtered)**: usually > 90 %
  of bases are kept.
- **Pairs removed because they were too short**: normally well under 5 %. A
  large fraction points to adapter dimers or very degraded RNA.

## Try it

Inside an interactive job:

```bash
module load trim_galore/0.6.10
cd ~/rnaseq_practice
D=/proj/phanstiel_lab/Data/processed/subsamples/rna/PE_100k/subsampled
trim_galore -o trim --paired \
  $D/sub_IMGL_RNA_MGL_F_Ab_24h_S_1-1-1_S4_R1_001.fastq.gz \
  $D/sub_IMGL_RNA_MGL_F_Ab_24h_S_1-1-1_S4_R2_001.fastq.gz
ls trim
cat trim/*R1_001.fastq.gz_trimming_report.txt | less
```

Then count the pairs before and after:

```bash
echo $(( $(zcat $D/sub_IMGL_RNA_MGL_F_Ab_24h_S_1-1-1_S4_R1_001.fastq.gz | wc -l) / 4 ))
echo $(( $(zcat trim/*_val_1.fq.gz | wc -l) / 4 ))
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Check your understanding

1. After trimming, R1 has 99,500 reads. How many reads does R2 have?
2. A read ends `...GCAGTAAGATCGG`. What will Trim Galore do?
3. Why is it important that HISAT2 and Salmon both use the **trimmed** reads?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## Answers

1. Also 99,500. With `--paired`, pairs are kept or dropped together.
2. Recognise `AGATCGG` as the start of the Illumina adapter and cut it (and
   anything after it) off, leaving `...GCAGTA`.
3. Adapter bases don't exist in the genome or transcriptome. Left in, they
   lower alignment and mapping rates and can cause reads to be misplaced.
:::
:::
